source.title: Cerebras-GPT: Open Compute-Optimal Language Models Trained on the Cerebras Wafer-Scale Cluster
source.authors: Nolan Dey; Gurpreet Gosal;  Zhiming;  Chen; Hemant Khachane; William Marshall; Ribhu Pathria; Marvin Tom; Joel Hestness

record.tranche_reason: The study explicitly reproduces compute-efficient scaling experiments using held-out Pile cross-entropy and a compute-optimal token-to-parameter allocation, on a new dataset and model family.
record.gate_note: Rows cover the study's own Pile test-loss scaling, token-per-parameter experiments, reported fit residuals, and downstream-average scaling. The Chinchilla degradation curve estimated from values read off another paper's figure is cited-work-derived, not a result of this study's own training runs, so it is not a row.
record.test_reason: The study trains its own GPT-like family (111M–13B) on the Pile at ~20 tokens/param. It fits a loss-vs-compute power law and checks a 13B run against a fit from runs up to 6.7B. It runs small tokens-per-parameter sweeps and evaluates downstream accuracy versus scale. These are its own results on V1, V2, V3 and V6.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors also give an explicit loss-vs-FLOPs frontier law (Eq. 1). They argue that combined training-plus-inference compute should set the model/data balance. Their claim that ~20 tokens/param is optimal rests on small runs whose differences are within run-to-run noise, together with Pythia and Chinchilla agreement.
record.recipe_differences: Uses GPT-like models and held-out cross-entropy with a compute-optimal scaling approach, but trains a new open model family on the Pile rather than the original studies' models and datasets; it also uses its own FLOP accounting and reports additional µP comparisons.
record.method_sensitivity: Parameterization changes loss deviations from the SP fit: reported standard deviation is 0.66% for SP and 0.04% for µP. The authors also report approximately 0.35% run-to-run loss variance for the small-scale token-per-parameter experiments.

fits_no_version.finding: Switching from SP to µP lowers Pile loss by an average 0.43% relative to the SP fit and cuts scatter about 16x. This shifts the level of the frontier rather than any measured exponent.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Parameterization and hyperparameter transfer (µP) shift the loss-compute frontier offset and reduce scatter around it.

record.problems: The scale sweep largely co-varies parameter count, tokens, and compute at a near-constant token-to-parameter ratio, so separate scaling exponents are not established. The token-ratio sweeps cover only 111M, 256M, and 590M models, their plotted values are not given numerically, and the authors say losses there are within expected run-to-run variance. SP models show substantially more variation around the fit than µP models.
record.rows_left_out: No separate rows for comparative GPT-J, GPT-NeoX, OPT, and Pythia losses or their downstream metrics; these comparisons are not needed to represent the study's own Cerebras-GPT scaling and optimum tests. Downstream task-specific scores are also omitted in favor of the reported downstream average. Full comparisons are in Sections 3.1–3.2 and Tables 2, 8, and 9.

untested.parts: Separate parameter-only and token-only power laws; the sweep co-varies N, D and compute at fixed ~20 tokens/param.
Extrapolation over orders of magnitude. The only check is 6.7B→13B (~3.7x compute, ~2x params).
Fitted exponents of optimal N and D versus compute. The optimum ratio is probed only at 111M–590M, so the Kaplan vs Hoffmann question is addressed only through a constant ratio.
Not tested; no fixed-parameter shape comparisons.
Not tested; no other modalities, repeated data or fine-tuning.
A quantitative mapping from pretraining loss to downstream accuracy.
Not tested. No comparison of fitting methods, parameter-count conventions, schedules or datasets on exponents or the optimal split, and no test of curvature away from a power law.

missing.what: The fitted frontier law L(f) = (f/5.984e22)^-0.0737 + 0.5066, giving the exponent and irreducible term
Loss degradation versus tokens/param for Pythia checkpoints the study evaluated itself. Degradation is smooth above 20; Pythia 12B at 25.3 tokens/param sits 0.3% above the frontier.
Pythia and OPT downstream accuracy frontiers deflect from power-law lines versus parameters
Five-shot downstream averages for Cerebras-GPT rise from 0.306 to 0.581 over 111M–13B
Per-size µP versus SP Pile losses

record.verdict_notes: R1–R6 are single points; the power-law evidence is the fitted Eq. 1, which no row records. The Chinchilla degradation curve fitted to points read off Hoffmann et al.'s figure is correctly excluded as cited-derived. Cerebras uses its own FLOP formula, which counts attention and softmax-V terms, and its own parameter-count formula; this matters when comparing exponents across studies.

versions.untested_parts: The main sweep changes parameters, tokens, and compute together at roughly 20 tokens per parameter; it does not independently fit parameter-only and token-only exponents while holding the other quantities non-bottlenecked.
Only the 13B run is explicitly checked against a fit from runs up to 6.7B; larger scales and other datasets are not tested.
The study reports an approximately compute-optimal tokens-per-parameter ratio, but does not estimate separate parameter-count and token-count exponents as functions of compute across a broad range.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or architecture at fixed parameter count.
No other modalities, repeated-data regimes, fine-tuning, or transfer scaling-law experiments.
The study reports downstream task accuracy against model size and compute, but does not establish a general quantitative mapping from pretraining loss to downstream performance.

The study compares SP and µP loss deviations from one SP fit, but does not systematically compare fitting methods, parameter-count conventions, schedules, datasets, or compute-optimal exponents, nor establish that curves bend away from power laws.
